source.title: FormalJudge: A Neuro-Symbolic Paradigm for Agentic Oversight
source.authors: Jia-Yi Zhou; Yang Sheng; Hantao Lou; Yao-Dong Yang; Jie Fu

page_placements.theme: Weak overseers detecting or resisting stronger models' deception, sandbagging, reward hacking and hidden bugs

record.file_problem: The full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses scalable and weak-to-strong oversight, but tests a formal judging system for detecting deception in stronger agents. It does not fine-tune a strong student on labels from a weaker supervisor or measure PGR.
record.gate_note: The paper's weak-to-strong result concerns a smaller judge detecting deception by a larger agent, not a strong student learning from weak-model labels. Its main benchmark comparisons and iterative-refinement results therefore do not test the listed claim versions. The adjacent deception-detection results are recorded as findings for none of the versions.
record.test_reason: The paper uses 'weak-to-strong' to mean a small judge (Qwen-2.5 7B) detecting deception in trajectories from larger agents (up to 72B) with a formal-verification pipeline. No strong model is fine-tuned on weak-model labels, and no weak supervisor, student or strong ceiling, or PGR, is measured. The original weak-to-strong concept appears only in a related-work mention, so the study neither tests nor uses the claim's setup.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that FormalJudge improves on LLM-as-a-Judge by 16.6% on average and lets a 7B judge detect 72B agents' deception with over 90% accuracy. They also report near-linear safety gains from iterative refinement with Dafny feedback.
record.recipe_differences: FormalJudge decomposes oversight into atomic facts and verifies their logical composition with Dafny and Z3; it does not fine-tune a strong student on weak labels or calculate PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: Agent capability affects the LLM-based judges' detection accuracy, while the authors describe FormalJudge as remaining above 90% across agent sizes with minimal variance across judge sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: A 7B FormalJudge judge exceeds 90% deception-detection accuracy on 72B agents' trajectories. LLM-only judges fall from 78–85% on 7B agents to 62–71% on 72B agents (Fig. 5, Deceivers).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Formal-verification-based judging lets smaller judges detect deception by larger agents more accurately than LLM-only judging, and its accuracy degrades less with agent size.

record.problems: The reported weak-to-strong detection accuracy is not a weak-label fine-tuning result and cannot establish PGR. The paper uses a frontier-model ensemble as its ground-truth judge; uncertainty for the specific over-90% result is not stated.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were extracted: the main benchmark comparisons evaluate FormalJudge against judging baselines, and the refinement results evaluate feedback-guided safety improvement; neither tests the listed weak-label fine-tuning claim.

untested.parts: No strong student trained on weak labels; no PGR.
No training-method changes to weak-label fine-tuning.
Judge and agent sizes are varied for oversight accuracy, not for PGR.
No measure of student exploitation of the supervisor, distribution shift, or error overlap in weak-to-strong training.
No theory of when a student must beat its supervisor.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only'. Weak-to-strong generalization appears only as a related-work citation and as a reuse of the term for scalable-oversight judging. Ground truth comes from a frontier-model 'God Judge' ensemble or from design-based labels. Table 1 uses Claude-4.5-Opus as the judge, not weak judges.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on weak-model labels and no comparison of a weak supervisor, weak-to-strong student, and strong ceiling.
No training changes to weak-label fine-tuning or PGR comparison.
No PGR analysis by supervisor/student size, task family, or representation. Judge and agent sizes are varied for a different oversight task.
No tests of weak-label student exploitation, distribution-shift effects on PGR, or error overlap between weak and strong models.
No theory of when weak-label students must outperform their supervisors.

rows.subject: Qwen-2.5 7B
rows.operation_detail: Used as the judge backbone in FormalJudge to detect deceptive trajectories from a larger agent.
rows.baseline: LLM-based judges: 62–71% on 72B agents, as summarized in Figure 5 caption
rows.note: This is weak-judge oversight of a stronger agent, not weak-label fine-tuning or PGR. The reported value is a lower-bound phrase; the baseline range is aggregated over LLM-based judges.
rows.check: Weak-judge oversight accuracy for a judging method, not weak-label fine-tuning. It is the study's own method compared with LLM-judge baselines, so it cannot bear on PGR. Subject and value are correctly read: Figure 5 gives FormalJudge at 91–96% and LLM judges at 62–71% on 72B agents.

relation.reason: The background discusses weak-to-strong generalization as an oversight challenge, and Section 4.4 applies that terminology to small judges supervising larger agents. This goes beyond citation but does not test the catalog's claims.

tranche.reason: Measures deception-detection accuracy using formal verification, without strong-student training on weak labels, PGR, or results testing V1–V6.

source_check.notes: The baseline range aggregates LLM-based judges; it is not specific to the 7B judge. This own-method comparison is contextual oversight evidence only. The recorded authors' conclusion matches the abstract and conclusion.
